channel.title: NewsCenter — Top 5 news of the day — 2026-11-16
channel.description: The five news that matter most today, chosen from Laurent's newsletters. 62 news received.

item.title: 1. Jensen Huang steps down as NVIDIA CEO after 33 years
item.description: Why it matters: Jensen Huang’s departure from NVIDIA after 33 years could materially affect the company’s strategy, valuation, and leadership of the AI-chip market. Jensen Huang has stepped down as NVIDIA’s CEO after 33 years. The planned succession and its implications for the company are at the center of questions.

item.title: 2. Anthropic’s IPO becomes a test for the entire AI sector
item.description: Why it matters: Anthropic’s planned Nasdaq listing and enormous supplier commitments will be a major market test of whether investors still accept the AI sector’s massive spending and losses. The creator of Claude is set to list on the Nasdaq at between 70 and 78 dollars per share, amid a difficult environment for AI and Nvidia. Anthropic plans to spend more than 900 billion dollars with suppliers despite a 104-billion-dollar loss over nine months.

item.title: 3. Washington prepares three bills to tighten AI chip exports to China
item.description: Why it matters: New US legislation to tighten AI-chip exports to China could reshape semiconductor supply chains and intensify technological and geopolitical competition. Following unproven allegations involving Jensen Huang, the US Congress is preparing three bills designed to strengthen restrictions on AI chips exported to China. None has yet been passed, and the details of the measures remain unknown.

item.title: 4. A compromised MCP server can hijack an AI agent’s other tools
item.description: Why it matters: The finding that a compromised MCP server can hijack an agent’s other tools exposes a serious security risk for businesses deploying interconnected AI agents. A test cited by VentureBeat found that a compromised MCP server could prompt an agent connected to five servers to misuse the other tools in 78.3% of cases. The article recommends limiting credentials, adding human approvals, and logging the entire call chain.

item.title: 5. Agility goes public as the first publicly traded humanoid company
item.description: Why it matters: Agility’s public listing makes humanoid robotics investable in public markets, despite its very small current revenue and substantial execution risk. Agility has gone public on the Nasdaq as the first publicly traded company specializing in humanoid robots, with a pre-money valuation of $2.5 billion. However, it generated just $1.8 million in revenue last year.
